Amazon’s electric delivery fleet
Can charging keep pace?

12 November 2026

Email
Share by email

Amazon says it has deployed 60,000 electric vehicles worldwide against its commitment to reach 100,000 by 2030. But the next challenge is bigger than replacing delivery vans: can fleet electrification cut emissions while maintaining delivery speed, cost and reliability as it expands into charging, heavy trucks and the systems that support them?
Host Ed Crooks and regular contributor Amy Myers Jaffe, Director of NYU’s Energy, Global Climate Justice and Sustainability Lab, are joined by Emily Barber, Amazon’s director of Global Fleet, and Tom Chempananical, Amazon's Director of Fleet in the Americas. They explain how a sustainability commitment has become a broader effort to redesign commercial delivery around drivers, customers and operating costs.
Amazon reports that its carbon emissions per shipped unit have fallen 39 per cent since 2019. Emily says electrification is one major factor, alongside regionalizing the network so inventory travels shorter distances and using forecasting and routing to reduce unnecessary miles. The company says early total-cost-of-ownership results are encouraging, with lower downtime and mechanical costs, while acknowledging that the full economics will only be clear once vehicles reach the end of their lives.
The partnership with Rivian shows what that redesign can mean in practice. Rather than simply electrifying an existing van, Amazon worked with the manufacturer on a vehicle built around the delivery day, from easier access to the cargo area to improved visibility and software that can evolve with operations. The bet is that driver experience, safety and operational improvements can reinforce the emissions and cost case.
Charging is a local infrastructure problem as much as a vehicle decision. Amazon shares a five-year demand roadmap with utility partners and installs chargers at delivery stations, while matching charge needs to routes and vehicle requirements. But grid capacity, utility rules and peak periods vary by site, and the company says finer-grained charging optimization is still developing. Emily and Tom also stress the less visible work: making fleet planning energy-aware, building public-charging backup and bringing repair, towing and charger-service networks along as deployments grow.
The discussion extends from e-bikes and other micromobility options in dense cities to electric heavy-duty trucks, yard vehicles and forklifts. Amazon is piloting across those harder-to-electrify segments, where range, battery economics and support infrastructure remain challenges. The test is not just whether an electric vehicle can do the route, but whether the whole charging and service ecosystem can support it at scale.
